topic: replacing a rotten garboard plank on a clinker dinghy and caulking the seams afterwards

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: wilgotnosciomierz do drewna

base: I am replacing a rotten garboard plank on a clinker dinghy that has sat under a tarpaulin for years.
A smaller dinghy stands beside it in the shed, and its planking is sound enough to copy.
I bought a moisture meter last month, because the timber in that shed never seems properly dry.
The new plank is oak, cut a little thick, and I have not yet begun any shaping.
Should I fit the plank first and caulk afterwards, or work the seams as I go?
Fit every plank dry first, because caulking a seam that still moves only wastes good cotton.
Oak takes up water quickly and will swell against its neighbours once the boat goes afloat.
Leave the plank a shade proud, then plane it fair after the fastenings are all home.
Only when the whole run lies sweet should you think about driving any cotton at all.
I hung the plank dry and it sits fair along most of its length now.
Near the stem it stands away from the hood end by roughly two millimetres, maybe more.
The moisture meter reads eighteen percent in the old timber and twelve in the new oak.
Do I steam the end to bring it in, or take the twist out with a plane?
Steam it, because planing a hood end thin leaves you nothing to fasten into later.
A rag soaked in boiling water and wrapped for an hour will soften oak surprisingly well.
Clamp the end home while it is hot, then leave it clamped until the wood cools.
Wet timber that dries under strain keeps most of the shape you have forced into it.
The steamed end pulled in beautifully and the plank now lies against the stem without any gap.
I riveted the whole run yesterday, working from the middle outwards as you suggested earlier.
The smaller dinghy beside it has seams filled with putty rather than cotton and hemp.
Should I follow that older method, or drive cotton into these seams the way you described?
Drive cotton, since putty alone cracks within a season on a boat that works at all.
Use a thin strand, laid in loosely, and set it with two passes rather than one.
A seam packed hard on the first pass will split the plank edge as it swells.
Follow with soft putty over the cotton, and let the whole lot cure before painting.
I caulked the garboard seam in two passes and the cotton went in evenly throughout.
Near the stern the seam is wider than elsewhere, almost three millimetres at the worst point.
I am worried that cotton alone will not fill it without being driven far too hard.
Should I add a second strand there, or fit a thin wooden spline into the gap?
Fit a spline, because a seam that wide will never hold cotton for more than a year.
Plane a tapered batten of the same oak and glue it into the seam properly.
Once it is faired off, the seam becomes a normal width and takes cotton like the rest.
Two strands driven into one gap always work loose, whatever the older shipwrights may claim.
The spline went in cleanly and the stern seam now matches the rest of the run.
I caulked the whole length afterwards and the hull rings differently when I tap it.
The boat goes back in the water next month, which still makes me a little nervous.
Is there anything sensible to do before launching, or should I simply let her take up?
Let her take up, but do it slowly and in shallow water beside the slipway.
Wet the inside with a hose for two days before launching, so the planks begin swelling.
Keep a pump aboard for the first night, because every rebuilt hull weeps at the start.
By the third morning the seams should be tight and the leaking will have stopped.
